#4792. Danielle Frankel Reimagines the 21st Century Bridal Store

After nearly 10 years in business, fashion designer Danielle Frankel Hirsch has opened a 12,000-square-foot location in Tribeca with interiors set to change the bridal game. To create the new space, which opened in early November, Frankel Hirsch worked with AD PRO Directory designer Augusta Hoffman and Studio Partners Architecture.

The nearly two-year design process is complete, and the Danielle Frankel bridal salon is now ready for appointments. “We’re finally at the point where my heart and my head have been,” says Frankel Hirsch, who worked with Hoffman on her previous Los Angeles boutique and New York City atelier. “Because this is our third space together, we can almost speak in shorthand now.”

Frankel Hirsch on the staircase wearing a shirt she designed from Fortuny fabric. Hoffman used the same Fortuny print throughout the space for wrapping side tables, keepsake boxes on the shelves, as well as for the woven seats on barstools.

The unassuming entrance to Danielle Frankel on Hudson Street

In the reception room just inside the street entrance, the desk is custom, the chairs are antique, and the custom pendant is by Jamb.

Hoffman worked with the artist Miriam Ellner to create eglomise paneling surrounding the staircase. “The eglomise is one of my favorite things because when we were working with the artist we worked so intimately with her,” Frankel Hirsch says. “We worked on the placement the way that we do our laces. We kept going back and forth with the drawings because I wanted it to feel like our lace placement.”

On a recent morning, a bride and her wedding party were busy in the VIP suite making a final selection. The beaming group entered the space through an unassuming brown storefront entrance on Harrison Street, its two large glass windows encased in a sheer linen. From there they ascended a staircase up to a large gallery with over 30-foot floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the streets below on two sides, and a hand-painted mural pattern above on the ceiling.

The interiors of the original 19th-century Queen Anne–style red brick building were transformed by Hoffman (full disclosure: I am writing Hoffman’s design monograph publishing with Rizzoli in Fall 2027) into a modern, elegant bridal boutique that honors the history of the original New York Mercantile Exchange, first established in the 1880s to keep the standards of the grocer business. “We wanted the space to stay pretty bright and focus on the architecture, but we needed a lot of seating,” Hoffman says. “There was a lot of pressure because we wanted it to feel like Danielle and we wanted to leave our mark on the space, but it’s also so beautiful as is and we didn’t want to have too many interventions that take away from that.”

The rug, vintage Dutch leather armchairs, and custom clothing racks create one of the four seated zones in the gallery area. The wall features antique mottled glass windows. “We wanted this wall to feel historically accurate,” Hoffman says.

The custom oak screen features shelves for displaying miniature gowns by Danielle Frankel. The shelves are lined in silver leaf. The antique stool is reupholstered in a Fortuny fabric.

The view of the gallery area from a second floor bridal suite. The vintage teak seating set is reupholstered in a fabric by Manuel Canovas and the glass cocktail tables and Fortuny wrapped side tables are custom. The custom window panels are by Augusta Hoffman Studio for Wovn Home and the custom curtain hardware are bronze leaves designed by Hoffman. Hoffman pulled the leaf design from the details on the columns.

What previously functioned as a large, open space with a small mezzanine, had little existing infrastructure–no electrical, HVAC, or plumbing—and is now an area where brides can plot as they make the most important decision for their wedding day. In the gallery, Hoffman created distinct zones where wedding parties wait before their appointment in a private fitting room.

Much of the furniture was sourced by Hoffman and Frankel Hirsch together on trips to Paris. Antique glass vitrines separate the space, which they included from the previous New York gallery and filled with Frankel Hirsch’s own family wedding photos as well as printed details brides can use for their fitting. One vitrine has a board layered with references of crinoline and interlining. Another has custom Danielle Frankel cufflinks. An oak folding screen lines one half of the room, with miniature gowns set on shelves lined in silver leaf paper. Custom parchment and cerused oak racks Hoffman designed to withstand the weight of a wedding dress line the floor displaying roughly 65 dresses from Danielle Frankel collections.

The reflection of the wall is seen in the mirrored structure designed to house the elevator bank and stairwell to the street entrance. A framed antique floral plaster relief is flanked with 1930s Italian wall sconces in patinated glass and metal.

The staircase and elevator bank within the mirrored structure. “We had to add the elevator for function and for code, and we were like ‘How do we take this existing architecture and put an elevator in the middle of the room?’” Hoffman says. “It feels super unexpected, versus trying to hide it, and you get to see more of the surrounding architecture and light in the reflection.”

The custom rug is topped with an antique stool upholstered in a Fortuny fabric, a 1950s chair, and a 19th-century English pine console table.

The view from the sitting area adjacent to a bar. The vintage teak seating set was among the first items Hoffman and Frankel Hirsch sourced for the space. The custom bar stool is woven with a Fortuny fabric.

The view from within the staircase to the gallery area. The custom center table is by Rafael Carneiro Triboli and the French chairs are from the 1930s.

Hoffman and Studio Partners Architects took what was formerly the mezzanine, originally separated from the below with only a single-bar metal railing, and made it into a full wall with antiqued mottled glass windows. In the center they constructed a cascading grand staircase, cleverly concealing the stockroom underneath, which leads upstairs to three private bridal suites. The hallways, painted in Wenge by Benjamin Moore, lead to the bridal suites, each designed differently and filled with antique and vintage furniture, custom carpets, lighting, and racks. The walls are painted in Presidente Roman Clay by Portola Paints, an earthy contrast to the white and ivory dresses, which are naturally the center of attention for visitors in each room.

When guests are finished in their suites, there’s a bar in the gallery space where wedding parties can sit and make the final selection. The wedding party that morning had selected the dress and were toasting champagne to celebrate. “It’s just as much about the hospitality and the warmth as it is about the gowns,” Frankel Hirsch says.

In the VIP bridal suite, which can be accessed through a discreet entrance on Harrison Street, the custom sofa is upholstered in Holland & Sherry’s Corbel in Henna. The artwork features fragments of 19th century Japanese brocade.

The midcentury armchairs are upholstered in a Watts 1874 fabric and flank a vintage oak table.

The rack, mirror, and ceiling pendant are all custom in the VIP bridal suite.

In the dressing area of the VIP bridal suite, the ceiling pendant is custom and the closet wall covering is by Watts 1874.

The 1930s lounge chair is reupholstered in a Fortuny fabric and the 1970s lamp is from Brazil.

#4790. ‘Dune: Part Three’: An Exclusive First Look at the Sets

Nothing about the cinematic language of Dune is small—director Denis Villeneuve’s film trilogy does span multiple planets, after all. But throughout his work on the movies, including the upcoming Dune: Part Three, production designer Patrice Vermette has made sure to stay focused on the little details.

“My approach has always been with symbolism and semiotics,” Vermette tells AD. “It is my philosophy of design, because for Denis, empty design cannot exist. Things need to have a purpose. Need to have a signification.”

In conversation with Vermette about the sci-fi epic, examples of that core tenet come up often. Carefully designed details imbue hidden meaning in each set, creating a captivating, immersive on-screen world that earned the designer an Oscar for his work in the first Dune. The trilogy’s latest installment, Dune: Part Three, which lands in theaters on December 18, expands on that ethos. And for the final film in the series, the sheer scale of the sets was larger. “It was our last chance working in that world,” Vermette says. “It’s like in a fireworks [display], it’s the end, it’s the bouquet final, it’s like, ‘alright, let’s do it!’”

Robert Pattinson as Scytale, with director Denis Villeneuve.

Over 450,000 square feet of interior stages and 475,000 square feet of backlots were used for scenes shot in Budapest alone, with each set typically taking 14 to 16 weeks to build. (Filming also took place in Abu Dhabi and Iceland.) Even the sandworms that slither through the titular dunes got grander this time around: Instead of the relatively small platforms that were used to film worm-riding sequences as in the previous films, the production team built a 300-foot-long by 65-foot-wide sandworm in the middle of the desert.

Like in Dune: Part Two, Vermette was challenged to create entirely new sets for this installment, which adapts Frank Herbert’s 1969 novel Dune Messiah. One of the new settings viewers can expect is Wallach IX, the home of the powerful and secretive Bene Gesserit sisterhood. Throughout their planet, Vermette incorporated stone etchings that resemble human cells seen through a microscope, referencing the Bene Gesserit’s breeding program that has gone on for millennia. Mother nature also informed the architecture. “When you arrive on the planet, the buildings are basically eggs of a spider, like crops of spider eggs as you find them in nature,” Vermette explains. “Ecology has always been a huge source of inspiration for me, and also for the storytelling it gives—you know, they’ve got their web across the universe, for the genealogy they create.”

Another new setting is the Veteran’s District, where the Fremen, the native inhabitants of the desert planet Arrakis, retire after fighting in the catastrophic holy war spurred by Paul Atreides, aka Muad’Dib (Timothée Chalamet). In the previous films, the Fremen lived in communal residences lined with hand-carved stone that recorded their history and culture. Returning from the battlefield, they find mass-produced housing units instead of the “green paradise” they were promised would await them. Made of ceramic instead of rock, with stamped-on rather than hand-carved markings, the Veteran’s District represents an artificial facsimile of their former homes. “And when you put all these units together, and you look at the rooftops, it’s there to represent sand dunes,” Vermette explains. “All these triangles align [to look like dunes], but it’s fake.”

Another circular doorway represents an all-seeing eye near the lush Imperial Gardens, which illustrate Paul’s extreme wealth and control of resources—including water—on the dry planet of Arrakis.

There is a green paradise on Arrakis, just not for the Fremen. Lush gardens grace the planet’s Imperial Palace, a massive inverted pyramid with a large circle cut out of it—a reimagined version of the all-seeing eye. “I got inspired by the title of the book, Messiah, and from the fact that Denis, just like Frank Herbert, wanted to make sure that Paul Atreides was not going to be seen as a hero, and it’s a tale of being cautious about messianic figures,” says Vermette. Similar representations of the all-seeing eye are found throughout the palace, sinisterly implying that Muad’Dib is always watching.

In actuality, Muad’Dib’s personal quarters are completely isolated from the rest of the palace. His wife, Irulan (Florence Pugh), must find her way through a twisting mass of hallways to reach him. “Basically, she’s walking into the psyche of Paul,” Vermette explains. “She goes into a void, and then it’s all these mazes of one’s mind.” When we get to the end of the maze, we see that Paul’s inner sanctum resembles a humble desert camp. Not unlike the Fremen, his dwelling has been reduced to an echo of what once was. He is “living as a recluse because he doesn’t trust anybody,” Vermette explains. “He wants to go back to a place where he felt the most comfortable, which was the desert. So he recreated that space.”

“Denis really wanted that set to be the golden cage of Irulan,” Vermette says of these private chambers. “She’s married to the emperor, but she’s not free at all, she’s a prisoner.” The window is shaped similar to an infinity symbol, but is covered in metal screens. “It’s like eternity, but eternity is blocked. It’s like a cage.”

The entrance to the maze within Muad’Dib’s inner sanctum. Vermette designed 40 maze wall panels that needed to be moved into various configurations to shoot the scene, which was filmed in less than a day. Eight people were each assigned a portion of the 12-foot-high panels and learned a choreography of sorts, quickly moving into each configuration until they could do each one in five minutes or less. “We rehearsed and rehearsed, just like dancers or musicians; they knew exactly where to fit their pieces” within the roughly 14,400-square-foot space, says Vermette.

On the planet Wallach IX, the office of Bene Gesserit Reverend Mother Mohaim features stone carvings inspired by human cells under a microscope.

The Imperial Palace throne room took 20 weeks to build. Behind Muad’Dib’s emerald throne, the windows are shielded with metal cast screens inspired by Montreal’s Saint-Ambrose Church, which was built in 1925 by architect Ernest Cormier.

The all-seeing eye is a repeating symbol Vermette inserted throughout the Imperial Palace, including a representation seen here as the circular entrance of Paul’s Keep.

The architecture of this Imperial Palace corridor has slanted walls to reflect a pyramid-shaped exterior and flying buttress support structures inspired by Gothic-style cathedrals.

#4788. Mel Robbins Started Lifting Weights in Her 50s. Here’s What Her Gym Routine Looks Like

The podcast host breaks it down on the latest episode of Strong Like.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Mel Robbins has always been a mover—running, hiking, skiing, Pilates, yoga, you name it—but it’s only been recently that the 58-year-old has added strength training to her fitness regimen. She credits Dr. Stacy Sims (a Women’s Health advisory board member) and Dr. Vonda Wright, both guests on The Mel Robbins Podcast, with finally persuading her to lift weights.

“They kept saying, when we reach a certain age, 40 and up, for us to start resistance training and with heavier weights,” says Mel, who had to overcome a few fitness myths to finally prioritize pumping iron. “I was nervous I would bulk up. That's a joke, because you know how much you need to train to actually bulk up? I wasn't going to be doing that.”

So what exactly does Mel do in the gym? She walked WH through a typical session for the latest episode of Strong Like.

Before Mel’s feet ever touch a mat, she makes sure to jot down—with actual pen and paper!—what she intends to do at the gym. “This will ensure that you actually do it, because if you're relying on this noggin up here, it ain't happening,” she says.

With her to-do list by her side, Mel begins her session with a warm-up. She runs through a batter of stretches that include inchworms (with an added push-up—go Mel!) and lunges with a twist, before moving on to a banded overhead press to mobilize her shoulders. “I've stopped judging these little bands,” Mel says. “These little suckers look like nothing. Let me tell you, there's a whole lot of something in these bands. You'll be shocked at how much gain you can get and how great this is for you.”

With her warm-up complete, she moves on to the workout, shifting the bands from her arms to her legs for a duck walk. Mimicking the water fowl, she moves forward and back, side to side, keeping outward pressure on the bands.

Next, she tackles one of her favorite moves, a reverse lunge with medicine ball twist. “It's a compound movement that works mobility, your core, your arms, your legs, everything in one movement,” Mel says. “It's super-simple, painful, and awful, and it works like a charm.”

She moves on to the upper body with chest presses, though she has a hack for lighting up even more muscles in the process. “If you want to maximize what you're doing here, suck in your stomach and clench your butt, because then it's not just arms; it's a whole-body thing,” she says.

Finally, she concludes with a snatch, joking: “You can work out a lot of aggression at the world doing [these].”

Ultimately, says Mel, her approach to fitness is pretty straightforward: “I'm not in here because I want to look good in a bathing suit. I do, but that's not the motivation. I'm in here lifting weights because I want to live a long, vibrant, healthy life. I want to be dancing into my late 90s. I want to make sure I can pick up the suitcase and put it up in the overhead. I want to make sure that I am strong so my life is long.”

To hear more about Mel’s gym motivation, click play on the latest episode of Strong Like above!

#4787. Can Non-Alcoholic Drinks Help You Stop or Reduce Drinking?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

The New Year is just around the corner, and it is a common time for people to revisit self-improvement-related goals. If you want to reduce or stop drinking alcohol, you may be wondering if switching to non-alcoholic drinks could be helpful. As it turns out, for some people, non-alcoholic drinks could be a helpful substitute for alcoholic beverages, but there are also reasons to be cautious about this overall approach.

Before reading this post, if you are not already familiar with non-alcoholic drinks, take a look at my recent post, “Is there alcohol in non-alcoholic drinks?” The short answer is that the amount of alcohol depends on where you live. Generally, non-alcoholic drinks contain much lower alcohol by volume (ABV) than traditional alcoholic drinks, but they may still contain some alcohol. If you are trying to stop drinking alcohol completely, it would be important to check the rules where you live to make sure your chosen non-alcoholic drink has 0% ABV.

There are many reasons why someone may want to stop or reduce drinking alcoholic drinks, which I will not go over here. More relevant to this topic are the reasons why someone would want to consume non-alcoholic drinks, which are made to look and taste like alcoholic beverages, rather than traditional beverages that do not resemble alcoholic beverages (e.g., soft drinks, juices, water).

One reason for the popularity of non-alcoholic drinks is that someone may enjoy the taste of alcoholic drinks, like beer and wine, and wish to continue to drink similarly flavoured beverages (without the risks associated with consuming alcohol). Another reason people may choose non-alcoholic drinks is that they find it helps them continue to participate in social activities and routines that typically involve alcohol. For instance, when interviewing adults who drink alcohol heavily and have used non-alcoholic drinks to reduce drinking, some interviewees described that ordering a non-alcoholic beverage at a bar, club, or other social gathering allowed them to participate in the outing and blend in with their peers who were drinking alcohol.1 Further, unlike drinking alternatives like soft drinks, they describe that the experience of drinking a non-alcoholic drink remains symbolic as an "adult treat" given its look and presentation.

People may take different approaches to substitute with non-alcoholic drinks depending on their specific needs. Some people may completely substitute their alcoholic drinks for non-alcoholic drinks. Alternatively, people may replace alcoholic drinks in specific contexts, such as primarily substituting their home-based alcoholic drinks versus outing-based alcoholic drinks with non-alcoholic drinks.1 When replacing alcoholic drinks one typically consumes, some may replace them completely with non-alcoholic drinks while others may alternate between drink types (sometimes referred to as “zebra striping”).

While people describe using non-alcoholic drinks to reduce their alcohol use, an important question remains about whether these drinks can actually help you stop or reduce drinking. As it turns out, the qualities that make non-alcoholic drinks an attractive substitute for alcoholic drinks may also get in the way of successfully reducing one’s drinking. Aspects of drinking (beyond alcohol itself) can serve as powerful reminders—referred to as cues—of alcohol. Specifically, qualities of the drink like its taste, container, and where it is consumed can, in fact, lead to a strong urge to drink alcohol itself. By definition, non-alcoholic beverages will not lead to intoxication. Once consumed, these drinks may strengthen the desire to become intoxicated (rather than quench that desire), and lead someone to return to drinking alcohol.

Initial studies have suggested that non-alcoholic drinks may help people reduce their drinking. When adults who drink were provided non-alcoholic drinks free of charge over a 12-week period, they reported greater reductions in their alcoholic drink consumption compared to adults who were not provided these drinks.2 This reduction in alcoholic drinks continued a month after these non-alcoholic drinks were provided. A follow-up study suggested, however, that the reduced alcohol drinking was not observed amongst people with higher symptoms of alcohol use disorder.3 Additional research is needed to understand if non-alcoholic drinks may be a helpful way to reduce or stop drinking among people with an alcohol use disorder.

Ultimately, there would be a net health and mental health benefit if someone reduces the overall number of alcoholic drinks by substituting non-alcoholic drinks. For instance, if someone switches from drinking four alcoholic drinks per week to two alcoholic drinks plus two non-alcoholic drinks, they would be reducing their exposure to harmful aspects of alcohol. However, depending on an individual’s circumstances, the chosen strategy for which drinks to substitute can affect how much they benefit overall. For instance, if a person finds they have more difficulty moderating their drinking when out with friends (versus at home), having a strategy to rely on non-alcoholic drinks when out with friends may be more beneficial than substituting their alcohol drinks consumed at home.

While research is still in its early stages, non-alcoholic drinks show promise in helping people reduce their drinking. For some people, substituting non-alcoholic drinks may provide the benefits of drinking alcoholic drinks without the negatives; however, it is important to make sure the substitute approach does not become an add-on approach. In cases where non-alcoholic drinks are too similar to alcoholic drinks that it leads you to drink alcohol anyway, then the substitution approach is not successful. Therefore, if you are thinking about giving this strategy a try, it is important to keep track of your drinking carefully to determine if it is actually helping you to reduce the number of alcoholic drinks you consume.

1. Perman-Howe, P., Fenton, L., O’Donnell, R., Howell, R., Kersbergen, I., Clarke, Z., & Holmes, J. (2026). #4786. BYD is launching this 5-seat luxury electric SUV next week with over 1,000 km of range

BYD’s luxury brand, Denza, calls it “the king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles.” The new Denza N8 electric SUV will launch next week, offering an impressive CLTC driving range of over 1,000 km (621 miles), massive digital screens, and plenty of premium extras.

After opening pre-orders for the new 5-seat luxury electric SUV last week, Li Hui, Denza’s general manager, said the results so far “have been excellent.”

According to Li, the Denza N8 is “definitely the most anticipated luxury SUV of the year.” Using BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries, the Denza N8 EV has a pure electric CLTC range of up to 1,003 km (623 miles) on a single charge.

That’s just as much as the N8 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) it’s replacing, which offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

While Li confirmed last week that the new EV variant would go on sale in November, he didn’t give a specific date.

Now, it’s official. Denza announced on its Weibo page on Friday that the launch event for the Denza N8 EV will be held on November 12, 2026.

BYD is still offering a limited-time promo that includes a 5,000 RMB credit for those who place a reservation with a 2,000 RMB ($200) deposit.

The Denza N8 measures 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase. That’s slightly longer than the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

It’s available with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD version uses a single motor producing either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp).

The tri-motor Denza N8 uses BYD’s e3 platform. The setup includes three electric motors: a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, for a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

Regulatory filings earlier this year revealed it will use either a 130.15 kWh or 105.79 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 1,003 km (623 miles) and 800 km (497 miles), respectively.

The Denza N8 also features BYD’s latest Flash Charging technology, letting it recharge from 10% to 80% in just five minutes. It takes just nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Inside, the five-seat electric SUV features a massive 30″ infotainment screen that spans nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard, plus a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) at the bottom of the windshield.

Like most of its new luxury vehicles, the Denza N8 is loaded with BYD’s latest software and technology.

Added premium features include zero-gravity seating in all rows, a three-spoke steering wheel, wireless phone chargers, and ambient lighting.

The electric SUV is equipped with a roof-mounted LiDAR to support BYD’s God’s Eye 5.0 intelligent driving assistance system, plus its DiSus-A intelligent air suspension system.

BYD has yet to announce prices for the Denza N8 EV, but it will likely be slightly less than the N8L, an extended version that starts at 299,800 RMB ($45,000).

#4785. 41 Best Gifts for Women on All Special Occasions (2026)

The best gifts for the women in your life are probably right under your nose. Consider the unique facets of their personality, their hobbies, and what lights them up. Is it watching countless episodes of Barefoot Contessa, dreaming about an upcoming trip to the Poconos, sampling every kind of Sephora mini, or curating a high-design interior vignette? No matter the answer, a great present should match their energy to ensure they end up with something that reflects their essence and also shows you’ve been paying attention.

We’ve compiled a curated list of gift ideas tailored to all sorts of interests to minimize the guesswork for birthdays, Mother’s Day, the holiday-gifting scramble, and every momentous occasion in between. Our picks run the gamut—from home decor gems and high-tech gadgets to skin-care gift sets and culinary staples—but are still selective enough to feel special during the big unboxing reveal.

Silk pillowcases not only do wonders for your skin and hair, but they also make your bedscape feel more luxurious. Gifting her a set is a guaranteed upgrade to her nighttime routine.

A special pair of champagne flutes to mark special occasions and milestones will become a treasured fixture in her barware collection. This cheerful duo features bubbly glass adornments that will pair perfectly with a bottle of her favorite bubbly.

Receiving any Le Creuset cookware is a win for anyone who feels most at home in the kitchen. This Dutch oven is a treat that will become a staple for home chefs, who can use to make endless roasts, stocks, casseroles, and more. So as long as you’re invited for dinner, it’s a win for you, too.

Author Lydia Davis is best known for very short stories, some of them a single sentence long, but her essays are where the reader can see how her mind works. This first volume gathers five decades of writing on reading, translating, Proust, early tourist photographs, and the city of Arles. Complete the gift by dropping her off at a café, where she can read it while people-watching and underlining passages. Don’t forget to buy her favorite coffee.

No gift guide would be complete without a cozy blanket, and we’re making a bid on this mohair one. The colorblocked number is comfortable enough to drape over her shoulders whether she’s snoozing or curled up with a book.

A tablecloth is a smart gift idea for the singular reason that it’s not something you’d really ever buy for yourself. It’s delightfully multiuse: covering the many drink rings on your walnut table, performing as a park blanket in a pinch, and—most importantly—giving your favorite gal a sense of cohesive calmness as she sets her table.

Whether or not she has the dreamy silverware to match, Sabre’s serving set with trendy burgundy handles will feel like a little luxury for plating cheese boards and opening bottles. Elegant and slightly retro, they’re versatile enough to accompany both bold and understated tabletop decorations.

Paper napkins are fine for any regular evening, but a hostess deserves a beautiful set of cloth linens. Borgo delle Tovaglie, the Italian linen house Valentina Muggia took over from her mother, makes these in soft-washed pure linen. The red colorway is embroidered with an ivory floral motif that makes even takeout look planned.

“Few things are so favored in my home as this tabletop lighter,” says shopping writer Julia Harrison. “I got it on a whim, and then found myself using it routinely every night.” Perfect for incense, candles, burning cursed love notes, or enjoying a cigarette on the fire escape. Don’t forget the butane.

For the minimalist coffee lover who can’t resist a little chrome, Louise Roe has just the cup-and-saucer set to slide under the tree.

Enza Fasano works in the Apulian pottery tradition of Grottaglie, a town in Puglia, Italy. Her Guido cup and saucer bring the relaxed sense of a Southern Italian breakfast table to an ordinary weekday morning. The jade glaze is a staff favorite, and the set mixes with the line’s other colors if she wants to build a collection. Nota bene: It’s dishwasher-safe.

One thing about many a woman: She loves a pitcher. Not necessarily for pouring lemonade, but for the concept that she could, should the occasion present itself. These thick glass styles from Il Buco Vita double as great vases, too, making them a great hostess gift. They also hold plenty of water for her guests at one of her routine dinner parties.

If getting in a chapter or two of her current book du jour before lights out is a must, she’ll find a new best friend in this little task lamp. The head is magnetized, so you can direct light in pretty much any direction you choose. The sage shade has a notably relaxing quality.

No one has ever been charmed by a cardboard Kleenex box, which is what makes this such a satisfying find. Todd Nickey and Amy Kehoe designed the handmade lacquer tissue box with James Lowther of the Lacquer Company for a collection drawn from antiques they’ve collected over the years. The cover, made in Vietnam, slips over most standard tissue boxes. In khaki and chocolate, it will look at home on a nightstand or vanity long after cold season ends.

The year’s best photo deserves better than her camera roll. For the Ornament, Framebridge prints a picture you upload and sets it in a tiny frame on a green velvet ribbon, with a hidden pocket on the back for a note, then ships it in a vintage-style matchbox. It’s small enough to be a stocking stuffer and sentimental enough to hold its own among the bigger Christmas gifts.

A pair of candleholders from design giant Herman Miller (of Eames fame) is among the most affordable ways to say: “I think you have great taste.” If you feel inclined, you could tuck in a couple of her favorite scented candles to complete the gift.

This text that was pivotal in contemporary color research will surely become a favorite in her own book collection. Both visually appealing and full of knowledge, it includes 348 color combinations design nerds (like us) can use in their next project.

Rated the best overall waffle towels, this 100% pima cotton towel set is tested and loved by the AD staff. Their Imabari Towel Certification verifies they’ve been through the rigorous Japanese testing process for qualities of absorbency, durability, and craftmanship. After using them for a year, senior shopping editor Nashia Baker says “biggest perk is how much softer the towels have gotten after too many washes to count.”

If she’s the type to plan an entire trip around a hotel’s wallpaper, a Cabana Magazine subscription delivers three issues a year, focused on travel told through photography, writing, and graphic design. She’ll want it on her coffee table year-round.

AD’s Australian Open Door star Troye Sivan developed (and named) this sophisticated rose fragrance in honor of his sister, and chances are good the sweet story will resonate with the beloved female in your life. Splashes of myrrh and sugar bring a slightly smoky aroma to the rose base, while geranium and poppy add grounding floral notes.

Sometimes the smallest luxuries are the most impactful. Prada’s Sabrina Carpenter–approved lip balm is a pocket-size indulgence that reacts to your lip’s natural pH to bring a customized shade of pink to your pucker.

A compact blush in eight variations of pink is a can’t-miss contender in the makeup category. It’s a perfect stocking stuffer, and Violet Grey is the sort of cult favorite that will reflect your thoughtful gifting research.

Treat the woman in desperate need of a spa day to Nerra’s deep-cleansing bath system, which combats dull and dry skin with ancient Mediterranean self-care philosophy.

With four-layer organic cotton construction, luxuriously deep pockets, and a roomy, unisex cut, Boll & Branch’s cozy Dream Robe delivers on the promise of its name.

Merit’s two-piece gift set pairs one of its Signature Lip Liners with a coordinating Flush Balm (an everyday go-to for Harrison). There are seven pairing options, including two new shades, Cassis and Rose. The gift is an easy win for anyone whose makeup bag holds about three things, all of them good.

The gift of consistently good hair days? Priceless. La Bonne Brosse’s best-selling boar bristle brush is an indulgence that turns an otherwise unremarkable hair tool into an extra-special daily treat. It’s one of the few luxury gifts she’ll use every single morning.

Here, Laila Gohar reimagines the nougat comb in an egg shape with an elegant black tassel to boot. It also makes the perfect tool for a lavish updo. Made in France from Italian acetate, it’s a luxury piece she most certainly doesn’t have yet.

Five words: Soft, sleek, and machine-washable. A silk pajama top is a prime example of loungewear gone luxe.

These crisp-feeling, lightweight utility pants give the gift of effortless dressing. Available in a palette of classic neutral colors and rotating seasonal options, the relaxed shape and adjustable waistband of these cotton pull-ons make them an easy pick as a weekend staple. They’re also blessedly machine-washable—and she’s probably going to reach for them as soon as the dryer cycle ends.

This necklace-scarf hybrid can instantly upgrade any white button-down or basic black cocktail dress. The natural silk cord rests comfortably on the skin, and the kelp pendant proviess an ethereal touch that is elegant but slightly bohemian.

If you noticed her binging Love Story or pinning various CBK-inspired styles (that’s Caroline Bessett-Kennedy to you, gentlemen), this rollneck from J.Crew made the rounds on TikTok, Instagram, Substack, and beyond for its 90s-nostalgia look. It’s, at the very least, a sweatshirt upgrade.

This It-girl jewelry piece from one of Gwyneth Paltrow’s favorite brands includes not one, not two, but three rings fashioned together with 18K gold hardware—so it’s kind of like getting multiple gifts in one. The mixed-metal appearance is great if you don’t know her preference between gold and silver, plus the versatile design lets her wear it across multiple fingers or stacked on one.

Lizzie Ames modeled this sterling silver band on a strip of filet lace, down to the open grid pattern and the scalloped edges. It evokes a curated style that’s a little bit grandmother’s linen closet and a little bit art school.

The bigger the bow, the better. This silken black bag from playful brand Damson Madder is perfect for anyone who considers herself a loud but intentional dresser.

Ezcaray makes remarkable throw blankets, all hand-woven in mohair, but it’s sadly not socially acceptable to stay wrapped in one outside the home. Instead, buy her the miniature version: a plush scarf in a watercolor-like color palette to keep her warm all season long.

Cashmere sweaters are an obvious gifting move, but these gloves use the material in a surprising way. With the cashmere on the inside, under Italian-made suede, she’ll use them every day until April. The yellow-beige color is a great statement for under any of her big winter coats.

Erin Pollard started Underwater Weaving Studio partly because she found most basket-weaving kits dated and hard on beginner hands. This one comes with the materials and step-by-step instructions for a sturdy tote with two handles. So, after years of canvas tote bags, she gets a new hobby for the winter and a market bag she made herself by the summer. As unique gifts for women go, a weekend project beats another candle.

Here’s a journal that will actually motivate her to jot down her doctor’s appointments and after-work events lineup. She’ll have a hard time misplacing the notebook, thanks to the vibrant shade of blue, and you can add a personal touch with a thoughtful monogram or a horoscope emblem to pay homage to her birth month.

For the gal who has it all, a designer comb can travel with her anywhere—whether she’s jet-setting across the globe or just needs a touch-up between lunch and an afternoon work meeting.

She might have a lot of journals already, but she likely doesn’t have one that’s bound in ostrich-embossed Italian leather. The insert is refillable, so she can swap the pages once its weight or size gets unwieldy. Mémoire will hand-inscribe her initials, and it arrives in the brand’s keepsake packaging with a gift note included, which spares you an extra trip to the card aisle.

#4782. EVgo opens its first Tesla Superchargers, with hundreds more planned

EVgo has opened its first Supercharger station, and it’s in a Chicago grocery store parking lot. The site has 12 fast-charging stalls with both NACS and CCS plugs, and it’s the first of hundreds of Tesla Supercharger stalls EVgo plans to add across the US.

The 325 kW “EVgo Superchargers” are at Riverside Square & River’s Edge, at 3145 S Ashland Avenue. EVgo’s August announcement cited up to 500 kW for the Supercharger rollout.

The Chicago location features Magic Dock technology, which means both NACS and CCS vehicles can charge without an adapter. Drivers of compatible non-Tesla EVs can start a session through the Tesla app. If you drive a Tesla, the charging station shows up in the car’s navigation and Trip Planner. Other EVgo fast chargers with NACS plugs have been showing up in Tesla navigation since early September if you turn on third-party charging.

“By serving both Tesla and non-Tesla NACS drivers, we’re doubling EVgo’s addressable market and continuing to meet EV drivers where they are and where they want to charge,” said Badar Khan, EVgo CEO.

EVgo owns the Superchargers and self-brands them, and Tesla runs and maintains them. The first sites will be at Regency Centers shopping plazas with grocery stores.

Smart move on EVGo's part. More reliable charger at a lower cost than they can build themselves, and Tesla takes on all the maintenance and network operations for a slice of the sales.

EVgo is also adding NACS plugs to its regular fast-charging network, a rollout it started in 2025. The company aims to have 500 of those stalls across the US by the end of 2026, with Supercharger stalls counted separately. Over the next two years, it plans to put at least one NACS plug at every EVgo site built in 2023 or later.

#4781. 46 Best Gift Ideas for Men (2026): Presents That Won’t Disappoint

Guys can be disastrously tough to shop for, but the best gift ideas for men don’t have to involve a brainteaser. What do you buy for the dad with a fondness for practical things? Some elevated basics or tech essentials, not just another six-pack of tube socks, should do the trick. For the brother with a taste for the finer things? We’ve got some ideas of the luxury persuasion that don’t involve placing bids on Grailed or eBay. For the husband who claims to be OK with no gift at all (he’s lying), please resist the impulse to hit him with a gift card. There are several handsome layering options along with some cooking upgrades that will please even the man who struggles with paint-by-numbers meal kit recipes (ahem, a Japanese grater might change his life).

We’ve got a lot of covetable and cool gifts at every price point for Father’s Day, birthdays, and every ‘just because’ milestone in between. Light up his life with a Louis Poulsen fit for any modern man.

Balmuda’s incredibly stylish kitchen appliance guarantees perfectly toasted bread to pair with his morning cup of joe. #4780. What to Do When You’re Unsure About a Choice

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Many people struggle with making important decisions. These include which college to attend, which career to undertake, whether to look for a new job, or how to find the right house.

One way to settle on a decision is to make a list of pros and cons of a particular course of action. A cost/benefit analysis can also help: What would the cost be for a particular choice vs. the potential benefit?

For instance, here is a simple example: Suppose you are deciding between buying two houses that differ in price. The less expensive house will have a lower down payment that would allow you to have some money left in your savings account, but it is not in a great neighborhood. The more expensive house will drain your savings, but it is in a great neighborhood.

If the neighborhood is very important to you (great benefit), it might be worthwhile to drain your savings (cost). In other words, the benefit outweighs the cost. If the neighborhood is not that important to you, then the benefit of the more expensive house would not outweigh the cost, and therefore you should buy the cheaper house.

Sometimes, it’s hard to assess potential benefit vs. cost. For instance, if you are considering which college you want to attend, and different colleges provide different educational and extracurricular benefits that are hard to quantify, how do you make a decision?

When several colleges appear to be reasonable choices, I have a secret to share: It doesn’t matter which college you choose.

Among colleges that are a reasonable fit, what you do there matters more than which one you pick. As long as you work hard and take advantage of the educational and personal opportunities available to you at a college, you will gain a lot. If you don’t work hard and keep to yourself, you will gain little, no matter what college you attend.

Further, even if it were possible to make a “perfect” choice when you face a decision, within a few months the choice will no longer be perfect.

Because circumstances will have changed in a way that affects the benefits and potential costs of your decision.

For instance, if the decision you made related to choosing an undergraduate school, your preferences will likely change once you are exposed to new ideas, people, and situations that may alter your college experience in unforeseeable ways.

Bottom line: Even with important decisions, pick one, and make the best of it. In most circumstances, you will do well. If that does not turn out to be the case, you often can change course, and will have become wiser because you will be able to figure out how to avoid making a similar wrong choice in the future.

Another secret to keep in mind is: There is no "one" correct path for your life. People don’t click along straight lines like trains on railroad tracks. We float and bob and turn like rafts on a river that’s always flowing and changing.

You may feel like you can’t afford to make any “wrong” decisions—but sometimes the less obvious choice is a great one that will create new possibilities for you.

On my Center Point podcast, I have interviewed many successful people. I’ve been struck by many of the interviewees who changed course a few times until they identified their main career when they were in their late 20s.

Further, keep in mind that many people change jobs often, especially early in their working lives (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), so your first choice is unlikely to lock you in permanently. With these secrets in mind, let’s look at thinking patterns that can help make good choices:

Instead of asking, "What's the can't-fail choice?" consider asking, "What meets my needs?" Instead of "What could go wrong?" ask, "What are the possibilities? Instead of "What will everyone else think?" ask, "What is right for me?" When you ask these questions, you give your inner wisdom a chance to help guide you.

Some of the greatest blessings that come into our lives are surprises. When a decision doesn’t play out the way you want or expect, think about how you can embrace your new direction or challenge instead of ways you can be unhappy about it. For instance, when you decide to audition for a part in the school play and don’t get chosen, think of what you can do with all the free time you’ll have.

When you feel stuck about a decision, imagine how your future self will feel about your choice—maybe in a month, a year, or even 10 years. What advice would the future wiser, older version of you give? Let the answer help guide your choices today.

Did you know that there’s a scientific principle called the Batman Effect? It’s just as cool as it sounds. Also known as self-distancing, this is the idea that you can create a little space, perspective, and extra strength to deal with any decision or situation by getting out of an “I” mindset. In one study, researchers asked people to give a small public speech. (Speaking in public is a common and severe fear.) One group was asked to think about the upcoming speech as if they were in the middle of it, making statements that started with “I am” and “I feel.” Another group was asked to consider the same things, but instead of using an “I feel” statement, a participant named Anne would say, “Anne feels” or “Anne thinks.”

It seems like a small change, right? But the results weren’t small. Participants who used the third person were less afraid and anxious, and they gave better speeches (Streamer et al,. 2017).

In a study with young children, researchers found they could take this idea one step further by having kids consider what Batman would do. Kids who were thinking like Batman were found to have thought more clearly than all the other participants (White & Carlson, 2015).

This kind of thinking is not just for kids. Years ago, when Beyoncé was explaining how she gives commanding live performances, she explained that when she was ready to go on stage, she’d stop thinking of herself as a regular person and start thinking of herself as a strong, powerful performer called Sasha Fierce. Sasha Fierce was confident and bold, and she helped make Beyoncé one of the top-selling recording artists of all time.

Making important decisions can be stressful, especially when we worry that one wrong choice could change the course of our lives. But there is rarely just one correct path. By considering our options thoughtfully, asking ourselves helpful questions, and remaining flexible about what comes next, we can approach decisions with greater confidence.

Parts of this post are excerpted from my book, The Life Guide for Teens.

Streamer, L., et al. (2017). Not I, but she: The beneficial effects of self-distancing on challenge/threat cardiovascular responses. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 70, 235–241.

U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. (2025, August 26). Number of jobs, labor market experience, marital status, and health for those born 1957–1964 (USDL-25-1322). U.S. Department of Labor. https://www.bls.gov/news.release/nlsoy.nr0.htm

White, R. E. & Carlson, S. M. (2015). What would Batman do? Self-distancing improves executive function in young children. Developmental Science, 19(3), 419–426.

#4777. Hyundai’s $359 IONIQ 5 lease looks like a deal, but don’t overlook its bigger sibling

The Hyundai IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in America outside of Tesla, but its larger three-row sibling looks like the better deal right now.

Through September, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 was the third top-selling EV in the US, behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3.

Hyundai’s electric SUV is outselling rivals like the Chevy Equinox EV, Ford Mustang Mach-E, and Toyota bZ.

Why? For one, it’s one of the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at about $35,000, and Hyundai has been offering some of the most attractive lease deals.

After the $7,500 federal EV tax credit expired at the end of September last year, Hyundai responded by reducing prices on the IONIQ 5 by up to nearly $10,000 on some trims.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250. That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. Upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model adds $2,500, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row electric SUV, the IONIQ 9, starts at $58,955, or nearly $24,000 more than the base IONIQ 5 SE.

On Hyundai’s website, the 2027 IONIQ 5 SE Standard Range is available to lease from $359 a month. The offer is for a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing for an effective cost of $567 per month.

The extended-range Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE RWD can be leased from $369 a month. The offer is also a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing, for an effective cost of $577 per month.

Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9, meanwhile, is available to lease from $419 a month. That deal also includes $4,999 due at signing, but is for a 36-month lease, so the effective cost is $557 per month.

Using Hyundai’s payment calculator, it would cost about $412 a month to lease the 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE for 36 months with $4,999 due at signing. With an effective cost of $550 per month, it’s only $7 less than the three-row IONIQ 9.

The Hyundai IONIQ 9 offers more range than its smaller sibling, with an EPA-estimated range of up to 335 miles for the base SE trim.

The IONIQ 5 is a midsize electric SUV, about the same size as a Tesla Model Y, with two rows and enough room for five passengers. Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating and six- or seven-seat configurations.

With an added row of seating, the IONIQ 9 offers up to 163.54 cubic feet of interior passenger volume, compared with the IONIQ 5, which offers up to 106.5 cubic feet.

While the IONIQ 9 may be the better deal right now, the IONIQ 5 is still a good fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that doesn’t necessarily need the added space.

In comparison, the standard Tesla Model Y RWD is listed for lease starting at $499 a month with an EPA range of up to 321 miles. That’s for a 36-month lease with $3,000 down.

Using Tesla’s payment calculator, if you put the same $4,999 down for a 24-month lease like the IONIQ 5, the Model Y RWD’s monthly rate is $549.

Which one would you choose? The IONIQ 5, IONIQ 9, or Tesla Model Y? Let us know why in the comments.

Both the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are built at Hyundai’s Metaplant America outside of Savannah, Georgia.

I really haven’t seen much value in leasing. I’d rather buy the car outright using cash, with the goal of keeping the car for 10+ years.

My family recently bought a Hyundai IONIQ 5, and it is an outstanding car. Loaded with great features — both on the EV side and then for safety and comfort.

When we toured the facility earlier this year, Hyundai told us that its electric SUVs are attracting new buyers to the brand at a higher rate than its gas or hybrid vehicles.

The IONIQ 5 had a 69.8% conquest rate last year, while the IONIQ 9 had 64.3%. Hyundai’s Elantra N ranked third (61.9%), followed by the Palisade (61.2%) and Kona Electric (60.9%).

#4774. What “Food Is Medicine” Actually Means, According to a Cardiologist

Plus, Chef Marcus Samuelsson shares easy ways to sneak more plant-based foods into your diet.

Despite what fitfluencers and gym bros might have you believe, eating healthy is about a lot more than counting macros and calories. Every day, scientists are learning more about how our eating habits can influence health beyond just our weight, including blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and risk of developing heart disease.

That's part of the idea behind a buzzy approach to health care known as “food is medicine,” which contends that what we put on our plates can be a meaningful part of preventing and managing disease.

The challenge is understanding what actually helps and turning that knowledge into meals we want to keep eating. To unpack this, Future You host and editorial director of Men’s and Women’s Health Rich Dorment sits down with Marcus Samuelsson, the acclaimed restaurateur and author of the new cookbook, Back to Green, and Louai Razzouk, MD, a cardiologist at NYU Langone Health.

Here’s a look at some of the themes covered in the episode:

Samuelsson says that beso is an Ethiopian drink that combines roasted barley with water or milk of your choice. “You just shake it and this is the best protein shake you can have,” he says. You can find the more specific recipe in Back to Green.

He grew up eating foods like beso as well as shiro, a stew made from chickpea flour, and other Ethiopian “superfoods” that he incorporates into his dishes today.

Dr. Razzouk says it doesn't mean that you can treat a disease with food alone. “It does mean that you may be able to prevent it by having a healthier and more balanced diet, and possibly minimize how many medications you need to be on,” he says.

Dr. Razzouk says that while you may still need to be on medication, food can make a “huge” impact when it comes to managing conditions like diabetes or high cholesterol. “Food impacts our level of inflammation, our insulin sensitivity, our weight,” and our blood pressure, he says.

The first warning sign that a patient’s diet may be less than ideal is if they get most of their food from Uber Eats or another delivery service. “Most of the stuff that we order in, especially living in New York City, contains a lot of saturated fats, a lot of added salt, and a lot of processed food,” he says. He discusses a couple more red flags in the episode, including meal timing.

In his early 20s, traveling in Southeast Asia and Singapore opened his eyes to a new way of eating—and the idea that there’s great food to be found all over the world.

A plant-forward diet doesn't have to exclude animal protein, he says, pointing to the Mediterranean and DASH diets as examples of eating plans that incorporate some meat. “What I tell patients is that typically if you have a choice between getting a source of protein from an animal source versus from plants, then I would try to get it from plants,” he says.

“What I tell patients is that I want you to enjoy your life,” Dr. Razzouk says, adding that fad diets typically don’t work. “What we would like you to do is find a balance,” he says, eating in a way that's enjoyable and that benefits your health.

It's a lentil salad with a coconut turmeric vinaigrette—and Samuelsson breaks down why the flavors work so well together, plus ingredients you may have in the fridge or pantry that can level it up even further.

He’ll often bring home new ingredients (e.g. spirulina) and encourage his son to look up the health benefits before they cook with it together.

Dr. Razzouk says diets high in fiber not only may lower your risk of colon cancer, but they also may lower your level of LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which impact your risk of cardiovascular disease. It also helps keep you full.

Cooking together can be an enjoyable family activity, Samuelsson says. “When I cook waffles and pancakes with my kids, we have fun,” he says. “The kitchen is a mess, but iPads are down, we're spending time together.”

Samuelsson suggests chickpeas, sea moss, and the fruit soursop. Dr. Razzouk suggests nuts (walnuts in particular) and extra-virgin olive oil.

Caitlin is a health and fitness journalist based in New York City. She writes for publications including The Wall Street Journal and Runner’s World. She's completed 12 marathons, including the six World Marathon Majors, is semi-fluent in French, and volunteers as a greeter on The High Line. Follow her on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#4773. Apollo’s newest electric scooter is also its lowest-cost yet

Apollo has spent the last several years carving out a spot for itself toward the more premium end of the electric scooter market. Now the company is trying something different: going after the mass market with its least expensive model yet.

The new Apollo Dash carries a $699 MSRP, but is launching at $599 as part of the company’s Black Friday sale running through November 30. More importantly, Apollo says the Dash isn’t intended to simply be a stripped-down budget scooter, but rather a way to bring much of its existing technology down to a lower price point.

The scooter uses a 48V electrical system powering a 600W nominal, 1,200W peak-rated Bosch motor, with a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h). Its 480Wh battery is rated for up to 25 miles (40 km) of range in Eco mode.

Apollo also claims the 48V architecture avoids limiting motor power to anemic levels as the battery drains, meaning riders shouldn’t experience the same increasingly sluggish performance toward the bottom of the battery that can occur on some lower-cost scooters.

At 43 lb (19.5 kg), the Dash is reasonably portable, though getting the weight and price down comes with an important compromise: there’s no suspension. Apollo also caps rider weight at 220 lb (100 kg), and points heavier riders or those regularly tackling rough roads and hills toward the more expensive Apollo Go instead.

Despite the lower price, there’s still a surprisingly long feature list. The Dash gets IP66 water resistance, self-healing tubeless tires, regenerative braking, built-in turn signals, Apollo’s Beam stem light, NFC unlocking, Apple Find My integration, and connectivity with the Apollo smartphone app.

Apollo says it put the frame through 10,000 km (6,200 miles) of durability validation before shipping production units. A beta test program also accumulated 1,002 miles over 144 rides without any reported punctures or maintenance issues. Beta riders averaged 19 miles (30 km) per ride while finishing with 29% battery remaining, according to Apollo.

Perhaps the bigger story here, though, is where Apollo is positioning the Dash. The company says 52% of its customers previously owned scooters from brands including Segway, NIU, and Xiaomi, but historically moving up to an Apollo often meant crossing the $1,000 mark.

At $599, the Dash appears designed to get those riders into Apollo’s ecosystem much earlier – while also putting the company squarely into competition with the mass-market scooters it previously sat above.

And for those wanting a bit more power or features, Apollo’s more upmarket models are on sale now as part of early Black Friday promotions.

November is National Adoption Month, a time when we celebrate families formed through adoption and acknowledge there are children who still need safe, loving, permanent homes. Yet adoption is more than the creation of a new family. It also involves separation, loss, unanswered questions, and the lifelong search for self.

Every adoption carries a responsibility to help children understand their story, not simply how they joined their adoptive family, but what happened before. Children do not enter adoption with a blank slate. A child's need to talk about adoption helps them make meaning of their experiences, build self-esteem, develop trust, and understand their identity.

When children are not given explanations, they create their own. I know this personally. I entered foster care at 15 months old and was adopted at seven and a half. I will never forget my adoption day. My foster-adoptive family drove me to the courthouse, and I refused to get out of the car. I wrapped my arms around the seat and held on for dear life, terrified that I was being given away again because no one had explained what was happening to me.

To the adults, adoption was a legal process for permanency. To me, it felt like another separation, another terrifying moment when adults were making decisions about my life without telling me why. This is why explanations matter.

Children need language to make meaning. Just because a child is not asking questions does not mean they are not thinking about them. Children will wonder: Why was I adopted? Why couldn't my birth parents keep me? What were they like? Did they love me? Are you going to give me away, too?

When these questions remain unanswered, children internalize the experience as rejection. They may conclude, I must have been a bad baby, or There must be something wrong with me. Young children are egocentric. They believe they are responsible for events happening around them. And they will equate that separation from their birth family means they were unwanted or unlovable. So, they need to hear repeatedly that the separation was never their fault. They did not cause it, could not have prevented it, and were never responsible for the adults' circumstances. As I often remind children, babies are simply not that powerful.

As early as possible. As soon as parents are educated, emotionally prepared, and have gained as much knowledge about their child’s history.

Adoption should never be presented as one dramatic disclosure. It is an ongoing conversation that must be revisited throughout childhood, a term called “recycling information.” At every new developmental stage, children will revisit facts with greater cognitive, emotional, and psychological understanding. Adoption is understood differently at age 4, 8, 12, and 16. New questions emerge as awareness develops, and information that seemed factual suddenly carries deeper emotions.

Parents should gather photographs, letters, birth information, and gifts the birth parent may have shared. Make copies of precious photographs so children can safely hold, explore, and revisit them.

Parents should become comfortable initiating conversations rather than waiting for their child to ask, gently following the child's lead, respecting their readiness, and answering only the questions they are asking, age-appropriately.

Ask permission before sharing sensitive details. "Are you ready to learn the answer to your question?" via The Question Box Intervention from my book The Traumatized & At-Risk Youth Toolbox. A child who receives difficult information may respond with anger, disbelief, sadness, or confusion. Try not to correct these reactions; acknowledge and validate how difficult this may be to hear. Remind them that you are available to listen and support them. Also, make sure they have downtime to process and integrate this newfound information.

Utilize my children’s book What Is Adoption? For Kids with an accompanying animation to begin the dialogue:

Parents can become anxious or uncomfortable when their child expresses curiosity about their birth family. Children are highly sensitive to these emotional reactions and may stop asking questions to protect their parents from discomfort. Some children may even fear that expressing interest in their birth family could threaten their relationship with their adoptive parents or lead to another rejection.

If you notice yourself becoming defensive, anxious, or threatened by these conversations, I strongly encourage you to work with an adoption-competent therapist. Your child needs to know that their curiosity is not disloyalty and that their birth family can be discussed without threatening their place in your family.

So, during this month, I encourage parents to remember that explaining adoption is not about finding perfect words or eliminating painful feelings. It is about being present when children need answers, even when those answers are difficult, because we cannot change what happened to them, but we can change how they experience their past by being emotionally available in their healing.

Eldridge, S. (2009). Twenty Things Adopted Kids Wish Their Adoptive Parents Knew. Delta.

Roszia, S., & Maxon, A. D. (2019). Seven Core Issues in Adoption and Permanency: A Comprehensive Guide to Promoting Understanding and Healing in Adoption, Foster Care, Kinship Families and Third Party Reproduction. Jessica Kingsley Publishers.

Smalley, B. K., & Schooler, J. E. (2015). Telling the Truth to Your Adopted or Foster Child: Making Sense of the Past. Bloomsbury Publishing USA.

#4770. 15 Airbnbs With Indoor Pools & Jacuzzis (2026): Top Summer Escapes

Airbnbs with indoor pools (especially the heated kind) are the kinds of “needle in a haystack” rentals that can save a vacation from feeling completely miserable in the coldest months of the year, or heighten the excitement of the enclave you’ve secured for a week of summer bliss. And though many of your standard Airbnb rentals will offer guests some generous amenities—a plush bed, a functional kitchen, and a high-pressure shower immediately come to mind—only a very select few allow you to book a pool that’s all yours (not shared, or fought over, by a bunch of resort guests). Better yet: There’s no “pool closes at 9 p.m.” signs.

But here’s the catch: The gap between a great indoor-pool rental and a truly tragic one is vast. We’re talking sleek, glass-wrapped sanctuaries on one end—and, on the other, a sad, chlorinated afterthought hiding in a basement with fluorescent lighting and 1994 motel energy. The good ones, though, have the power to allow you to lock in your vacation and tune everything else out. From a cedar-lined pool room with views of the surrounding forest to modern desert escapes where you can watch the sunset turn the surrounding mountains pink at sunset from your floaty, these pools make for an incredible retreat year-round, weather be damned.

Perks: Turkish steam bath, sauna, massage room, private chef, butler service, private backyard, security system

If your ideal vacation involves frescoed ceilings, crystal chandeliers, and a butler to fetch you juice that’s been freshly squeezed from the garden's citrus trees, Villa Dorata in Positano delivers. This five-bedroom Baroque-style villa is gloriously over the top, with jewel-toned interiors, gilded art, elaborate tilework, and terraces overlooking the Amalfi Coast. The private spa is an attraction in its own right, complete with an indoor swimming pool, Turkish steam bath, and massage room. Outside, lush gardens, fountains, and citrus groves provide plenty of places to enjoy the Mediterranean sunshine. There are even two traditional Italian pizza ovens for alfresco dinners. Daily breakfast, housekeeping, and butler service are included, so guests can spend less time managing the logistics of a group vacation and more time enjoying the villa's considerable extravagance. From $5,078 per night.

Perks: Jetted bathtub, private backyard, fire pit, outdoor furniture, pet-friendly, security system, free parking

Swimming season never ends at this three-bedroom home outside Binghamton, New York. The heated indoor pool occupies its own glass-lined space, supplying views of the surrounding trees and simulating the feeling of being outdoors. The rest of the house features vaulted ceilings, bamboo floors, and a contemporary mix of furnishings. Floor-to-ceiling windows let in plenty of natural light into the main living areas, and an expansive deck extends the entertaining space outdoors. There's also a balcony for morning coffee, a propane fire pit for chilly evenings, and a jetted soaking tub in the primary suite. With room for eight guests and a pet-friendly policy, it's a practical choice for a group getaway, particularly when the weather makes an outdoor pool considerably less appealing. From $425 per night.

Perks: Soaking tub, sauna, two fireplaces, private deck

The Catskills have no shortage of cabins with fireplaces and woodland views, but few come with their own indoor swimming pool. This four-bedroom getaway near Callicoon has all three, plus an infrared sauna for the ultimate wellness-centric stay. Cathedral ceilings, exposed timber, and two wood-burning fireplaces give the interiors a classic mountain house look, while oversized windows keep the surrounding three acres of forest in view. Outside, a path leads down to Callicoon Creek, and a generously-sized deck and fire pit make the most of the secluded setting. The house sleeps 10, so there's room to bring a crowd without having to share a hotel pool with strangers. From $410 per night.

Perks: Hot tub, spa deck, sun patio, grilling area, gourmet kitchen

There are indoor pools, and then there are homes built entirely around them. This sprawling five-bedroom retreat centers on a private heated mineral pool and hot tub housed in a dedicated spa space, turning a weekend getaway into something closer to a wellness retreat. Elsewhere, the home feels equal parts time capsule and thoughtful renovation. Original details—including a vintage intercom system, wood-clad ceilings, and dramatic stonework—sit alongside updated bathrooms and an eclectic mix of vintage and contemporary furnishings. Thoughtful extras—from a grand piano and art supplies to a gourmet kitchen and eight smart TVs—make it particularly appealing for multigenerational gatherings. From $945 per night

Perks: Indoor fireplace, private patio, dedicated parking, game room, wine cellar

From the outside, this townhouse looks like a regular Denver-area home. Inside, however, it’s organized around one genuinely unexpected element: a full-size indoor pool set beneath a ceiling of skylights and surrounded by greenery. A fireplace just off the pool deck gives swimmers a place to warm up between dips (or flips off the diving board). The rest of the house is built for groups who plan to stay put. Exposed brick and wood-paneled walls give the interiors a grounded, slightly retro feel, while oversized bedrooms and bathrooms make it comfortable for longer stays rather than quick weekends. A wine cellar and wet bar sit near the pool room, clearly intended for nights that stretch on, and a separate game room—complete with a pool table and shuffleboard—adds another place to gather. From $726 per night.

Perks: BBQ, fire pit, heated indoor pool, washer and dryer

Designed by architect Tomas Osinski, the home quite literally reflects its surroundings while an open plan setup connects one end of the space to the other—encompassing a lengthy 100-foot indoor pool, four bedrooms, and common areas dotted with modern furnishings from the likes of Piero Lissoni and Pierre Paulin. Staying here ensures a prime place for trekking out on hikes, while indoors you can take in wraparound views of the landscape while you swim laps in the deep end. From $2,333 per night.

Perks: Two game rooms, multiple smart TVs, fire pit, disc golf, covered balcony

Perks: Fireplace, breakfast nook, porch, farm animals

For a pastoral adventure with some thoroughly modern comforts, book this inn located on a farm 45 minutes out from Portland, Maine. Here, you’ll be occupying the cozy second floor suite, which offers a living room with a fireplace on cold winter nights and polished sleeping quarters. Perks: Game room, fireplaces, furnished deck, fire pit, movie projector

Perks: Home gym, game room, mountain and desert views

Guests have access to the entire home, which consists of four bedrooms and seven bathrooms—so go ahead and invite everyone on the group chat. #4768. Amazon set to deploy more than 3,000 TATA electric delivery trucks

Amazon isn’t just electrifying its American delivery operations. The virtual big box stores that Bezos built understands the benefits of EVs as well as anyone, and they’re working hard to deploy electric vehicles everywhere they can. And now, that global push is extending to India.

Indian automaker TATA Motors has announced a deal with Amazon to deploy 3,000 electric trucks across Amazon’s transportation network in India. When it goes live, it will be the largest electric truck deployment by in India and mark Amazon’s most significant move to extend its Indian fleet electrification beyond last-mile logistics.

“India is accelerating towards electric mobility and the realization of Viksit Bharat 2047,” says Shri H.D. Kumaraswamy, Hon’ble Union Minister for Heavy Industries and Steel, Government of India. “The collaboration between TATA Motors and Amazon shows what that looks like in practice: sustained demand from a nationwide logistics network met by electric trucks manufactured in India. Through PM E-DRIVE, the Government will continue to support this transition, and I look forward to more such efforts in powering green logistics.”

In addition to being a big deal for TATA, the 3,000 electric truck deal represents a serous bump to India’s deployed electric truck fleet, and are a major step towards the wide-scale electrification of freight transportation across the country – that’s not just good for Amazon’s fuel bills, it’s good for everyone and everything that breathes air, too.

“Electrifying our logistics and transportation network is an important part of Amazon’s goal to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2040,” says Abhinav Singh, Vice President, Operations, Amazon, APAC, Middle East, Africa and Turkey. “We have made significant progress in India, with more than 15,000 electric vehicles operating across 500-plus cities. To enable this transition, we are also supporting the development of infrastructure and solutions that make EV adoption easier for our carrier partners and drivers. We are now setting a bold vision to scale electric trucking, addressing one of the toughest challenges in decarbonizing transportation. Our collaboration with TATA Motors marks an important step towards realizing this vision. By combining our strengths, we aim to accelerate the deployment of electric trucks across more routes, starting with intracity operations and expanding to India’s major freight corridors.”

The truck Amazon will be deploying in these record numbers is a version of the Tata Ultra E.7, a 7.5-tonne (~16,000 lb.) straight truck powered by a 240 kW (~320 hp) electric motor drawing power from a 96 kWh LFP battery pack. The truck’s makers claim a loaded range of up to 130 km (~80 miles) on a single charge, with DC fast-charging that’s capable enough to keep the trucks charged up between deliveries.

Amazon’s new TATA electric delivery trucks will support the transport of goods between warehouse facilities – which means traveling across cities and along India’s national freight corridors.

#4765. Kacey Musgraves Is Hanging Her Cowboy Hat in Mexico These Days

Kacey Musgraves may be a Nashville staple with deep Texas roots, but the country star is calling a new locale home lately. The “Rainbow” singer, who has resided in the Music City for many years, revealed in a recent interview that she now lives in Mexico “most of the time.”

Musgraves told People that the change of scene “ended up just completely changing my life and inspiring me so much. I’m so in love with so many aspects of it, and it’s really taught me a lot.” She explained that the transition took place over a year and a half ago when “this beautiful cosmic thing” drew her down to Mexico. Living there with her Australian cattle dog Pepper, the singer-songwriter found comfort in a slower pace of life, which has allowed her to be barefoot often and to spend plenty of time outdoors. The relocation even moved Musgraves to release a sister album to her most recent, Middle of Nowhere Vol. 2: Tex Mex Tapes, which will feature four songs in Spanish.

Musgaves previously opened up about her wanderlust and the possibility of leaving Nashville for the bright lights of New York City. “Girl, I’m always browsing Zillow late at night, acting like a fool—it’s my favorite,” she told People in 2024. “I wouldn’t rule [moving] out, but I do have a community in Nashville that I know that I couldn’t find anywhere else.”

Back in 2022, the country queen and her 3,500-square-foot Nashville home graced AD’s May 2022 cover. She purchased the property in 2020 during a time of big changes in her life, which included her split from singer-songwriter Ruston Kelly. Still, she made it clear that the blank canvas was no “divorce house.”

“I wanted a place that felt like me,” she said, “where I could express myself without having to think about another person and what they might want. This felt like a new beginning.” Musgraves went on to sell that space and ultimately bought a “cottage” in the Tennessee forest.
